extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art and literary criticism; artists, sculptors and poets interested in Renaissance aesthetics and Michelangelo
extracted.subtask_short: critique of Michelangelo's art and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Close critical analysis of Michelangelo (and fifteenth-century Tuscan sculptors), enumerating aesthetic qualities and techniques valued in sculpture, painting and poetry (e.g., individuality, incompleteness, sweetness+strength, suggestion of life). Useful for critics, artists, and students assessing or emulating that style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality and intensity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: "Work which did not bring what was inward to the surface, which was not concerned with individual expression, with individual character and feeling, the special history of the special soul, was not worth doing at all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic values art that reveals inward experiences and the special history of a particular soul; individuality and intense, personal expression are primary merits. Example: fifteenth-century Tuscan sculptors and Michelangelo prize the 'impress of a personal quality.' Anti‑pattern: work that is merely generic, outward, or impersonal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of hard realism (avoid caricature)
rubrics_metrics.description: "He avoided a too hard realism, that tendency to harden into caricature which the representation of feeling in sculpture must always have."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation of feeling should not be made rigid or over-determined; realism that hardens expression into caricature diminishes the work. Michelangelo avoids over-finish to prevent this. Anti‑pattern: over-finished, literal depiction that kills subtle feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studied incompleteness as a means to suggest life (Michelangelo's 'equivalent for colour')
rubrics_metrics.description: "Leaving nearly all his sculpture in a puzzling sort of incompleteness, which suggests rather than realises actual form... that incompleteness is Michelangelo's equivalent for colour in sculpture; it is his way of etherealising pure form... communicating to it breath, pulsation, the effect of life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate partial finish/half-emergent forms invite the spectator to complete them mentally and impart vitality; rough‑hewn areas paired with delicate finish create pulsation and 'breath.' Example: comparison with the Venus of Melos; the David with a morsel of uncut stone. Anti‑pattern: completing every detail so the work loses its suggestive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine passion/intensity with yielding and flexible life
rubrics_metrics.description: "He combines the utmost amount of passion and intensity with the sense of a yielding and flexible life: he gets not vitality merely, but a wonderful force of expression."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful emotional charge must be balanced by a sense of pliancy or life — intensity without rigidity. Aim for both force and a responsive, living quality in form and gesture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective abstraction / conventionalism and use of low relief
rubrics_metrics.description: "Their way of extracting certain select elements only of pure form and sacrificing all the rest... a system of conventionalism... subduing all such curves as indicate solid form, and throwing the whole into lower relief."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good sculpture may abstract or omit non-essential elements, reducing modelling and using low relief to emphasize chosen forms and repose. Example: Luca della Robbia and other Tuscan sculptors extract 'select elements' and place them in lower relief to unite repose and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of colour and medium innovation (bringing high qualities into common things)
rubrics_metrics.description: "He became desirous to realise the spirit and manner of that sculpture... in a humbler material, to unite its science... to the homely art of pottery... instead of making his figures of baked earth simply white, he added the further invention of giving them colour... keeping mostly to blue and white, the colours of the Virgin Mary."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovation in medium (e.g., polychromy on earthenware) can transfer high artistic qualities into everyday objects; use colour judiciously and often sparingly to suit subject and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impress of a personal quality / intimité / profound expressiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The impress of a personal quality, a profound expressiveness, what the French call intimite... the seal on a man's work of what is most inward and peculiar in his moods, and manner of apprehension."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hallmark of great work is a distinctive personal tone or intimacy that reveals the maker's inward life; this originality/intimacy is rare and highly valued. Works lacking a personal seal feel less compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of sweetness and strength (lovely strangeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sweetness and strength, pleasure with surprise, an energy of conception which seems at every moment about to break through all the conditions of comely form..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should combine an energizing, sometimes startling strength with a sweetness or charm so the 'strangeness' remains attractive. Anti‑pattern: strength without sweetness (repellent/monstrous) or sweetness without force (insipid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give pleasure and exert a charm as well as excite or surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: "That they shall excite or surprise us is indispensable. But that they shall give pleasure and exert a charm over us is indispensable too."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works must both astonish and please; surprise alone is insufficient. Aim for loveliness alongside originality. Anti‑pattern: clever or shocking work that fails to charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic sweetness, not dependence on accessories
rubrics_metrics.description: "The austere genius of Michelangelo will not depend for its sweetness on any mere accessories... The world of natural things has almost no existence for him."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sweetness should emerge from the work itself rather than from added accessories or picturesque background elements. Rely on internal compositional and expressive means rather than external ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of the creation/suggestion of life (especially the human figure)
rubrics_metrics.description: "For him... the creation of life itself in its supreme form, off-hand and immediately, in the cold and lifeless stone... The brooding spirit of life itself is there; and the summer may burst out in a moment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chief aim is to evoke the animation of the human figure — to suggest life springing from inert material. Works centered on the animation or 'creation' of man are especially prized (examples: Creation of Adam, Leda, Adam in Sistine Chapel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of incompleteness to secure ideality (spectator completion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "He secures that ideality of expression which in Greek sculpture depends on a delicate system of abstraction... by an incompleteness... and trusts to the spectator to complete the half-emergent form."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate omission or abstraction invites the viewer to supply ideal form, producing a more universal, abstract beauty. This is an aesthetic device to achieve ideality rather than literal finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preoccupation with death, dignity and the expression of pity
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the great Florentines were preoccupied with death... Of all this sentiment Michelangelo is the achievement; and first of all, of pity. Pieta—pity—the pity of the Virgin Mother over the dead body of Christ... mere human nature therefore which has prompted the sentiment here."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious art engages with mortality, dignity in death, and evokes pity and tender sorrow (Pietà). Depicting death with restraint and human sympathy confers distinction and depth; anti‑pattern: morbid, grotesque or trivialized treatments of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatricality; preserve grave, temperate sweetness
rubrics_metrics.description: "His professed disciples... are in love with his strength only, and seem not to feel his grave and temperate sweetness. Theatricality is their chief characteristic; and that is a quality as little attributable to Michelangelo..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake raw force for the master's manner; theatricality (overblown gesture/drama) is regarded as a failing. Strive for seriousness and tempered sweetness rather than spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcend outward beauty to apprehend unseen/universal form (Platonic aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: "He is always pressing forward from the outward beauty... to apprehend the unseen beauty; trascenda nella forma universale -- that abstract form of beauty, about which the Platonists reason."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should move beyond mere surface prettiness to express universal, abstract forms of beauty or the 'unseen' ideal. The Platonic impulse elevates art from appearance to essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled convulsive energy (energy that must be moderated)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The presence of a convulsive energy in [medieval art]... becoming in lower hands merely monstrous or forbidding, but felt, even in its most graceful products, as a subdued quaintness or grotesque."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An energetic, convulsive quality can animate work but must be controlled; left unchecked it becomes monstrous. Aim for energy tempered by grace and sweetness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and austerity of presentation (avoid unnecessary ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Simple persons... who wore no gold on their garments"; 'no lovely natural objects... but only the austere truths of human nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity of costume, ornament, and background can heighten seriousness and truth. Restraint in decoration keeps focus on the human form and moral sentiment rather than surface display.
